narrative:
The model estimates a 61% chance that you will fail your final year, so it treats failure as more likely than passing and therefore requires remedial courses. This is not a certainty—there is still a meaningful chance you pass—but the prediction is strong enough that additional support is being required.

The main reason is your history of one past class failure. This was by far the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failing; students who passed had an average of no past failures. Two other factors worked in your favor but were not enough to offset that history. Your free time after school is low, which the model associated with passing rather than failing; passers more often report medium free time. You also want to continue to higher education, as did all students who passed, and this pushed toward passing. So the model sees a student with a protective goal and limited free time, but a prior failure remains the dominant warning sign.

To improve your chances, focus on avoiding another failed subject. Your weekly study time is under two hours, while most passing students study two to five hours, so a more regular study routine is the clearest practical step. You also receive no school or family educational support, so ask your guardian and teachers for structured help, and use the remedial courses to address the subject you previously failed.
